dataset.what_one_row_represents: A single noise-related 311 service request filed with New York City between 2023-01-01 and 2024-12-31, including who responded, when it was closed, where it occurred, and the resolution text.
dataset.geographic_scope: All five boroughs of NYC. 230 distinct ZIP codes appear. 99.96% of rows carry a valid ZIP; 0.04% are unspecified.

ana_01.label: Dataset scale
ana_01.content: Two full calendar years of noise-related 311 service requests yields 1,439,558 rows — every formally filed noise complaint in New York City between 2023-01-01 and 2024-12-31. The data is unusually tidy for a city open-data dump: eight values of complaint_type, 31 descriptors, 230 distinct ZIP codes, and only four responding agencies (NYPD, DEP, EDC, and a single ghost row coded to 3-1-1 itself).

complaint_type values: 8
descriptor values: 31
distinct ZIP codes: 230
distinct responding agencies: 4

data_table.description: Headline counts for the dataset

ana_02.label: Year-over-year: noise complaints rose 9.8% from 2023 to 2024
ana_02.content: Noise complaints rose from 686,283 in 2023 to 753,275 in 2024 — a 9.8% year-over-year increase and an extra 67,000 complaints. The 2024 average is 2,058 complaints per day (2024 was a leap year), versus 1,880 per day in 2023. (Note: this figure is below the 19% year-over-year jump some 2024 press coverage reported, because press counts often draw a slightly different filter from the same dataset.)

ana_03.label: Daily volume — median 1,684, max 8,820 on a Sunday in September 2024
ana_03.content: The typical day in 2023–2024 sees 1,684 noise complaints (median), 1,969 on average. The quietest day in the entire window was Monday 2023-01-23 with 830 complaints; the noisiest by a huge margin was Sunday 2024-09-15 with 8,820 — more than five times a normal day. Most of the top-10 noisiest days fall in late 2024 in the Bronx (see ana_24).

ana_04.label: Complaint-type ranking — Residential is half of everything
ana_04.content: Noise – Residential is by far the largest bucket at 47.1% of all complaints (677,749). Street/Sidewalk noise is second at 21.6% (310,450), Commercial third at 9.5% (136,096), the generic 'Noise' top-level (which mostly contains construction-noise descriptors) is fourth at 7.5%, Vehicle is fifth at 6.9%, Helicopter sixth at 6.1%, then a small Park slice (1.2%) and an even smaller House of Worship slice (0.18%). The two top categories together — Residential plus Street — are 69% of every formal noise grievance in New York.

ana_05.label: Top descriptor — 'Loud Music/Party' is 54% of all noise complaints
ana_05.content: One descriptor dominates the dataset: 'Loud Music/Party' accounts for 777,689 complaints — 54.02% of every noise filing across all eight complaint types. 'Banging/Pounding' is second at 15.5% (223,384), 'Loud Talking' third at 8.9% (127,548), and 'Car/Truck Music' fourth at 4.5% (64,847). Within each major category the dominant descriptor is even more concentrated: 80.5% of Commercial complaints are Loud Music/Party, 79.1% of Street/Sidewalk, 62.4% of Vehicle is specifically Car/Truck Music, and 97.2% of Helicopter complaints are the catch-all 'Other'. The generic 'Noise' top-level is the construction bucket: 41% is 'Construction Before/After Hours (NM1)' and 15% 'Construction Equipment (NC1)'.

ana_06.label: Agency split — NYPD owns 86% of noise, EDC quietly owns helicopter
ana_06.content: Three real agencies share the workload, and the split is one-to-one with the complaint_type: NYPD takes 1,243,510 complaints (86.4%) — every Residential, Street/Sidewalk, Commercial, Vehicle, Park, and House-of-Worship request. DEP takes 108,234 (7.5%) — the entire generic 'Noise' bucket, which is essentially all construction-noise descriptors. EDC (the city's Economic Development Corporation, which owns the heliports) takes 87,813 (6.1%) — every single Helicopter complaint. One stray complaint in the data is coded to '3-1-1' itself.

ana_07.label: How complaints reach the city — online dominates, phone is a minority
ana_07.content: Although the citywide 311 stat is famously 68% phone, for noise complaints specifically the channel mix is inverted. 60.78% (874,940) come in through the 311 website, 26.76% (385,203) through the NYC311 mobile app, and only 12.46% (179,320) by phone. Phone is the minority — under one in eight noise complaints — and 'OTHER' / 'UNKNOWN' together are 0.01%. New Yorkers, when it comes to noise specifically, type rather than dial.

ana_08.label: Channel shift 2023 → 2024 — online down 15 pp, mobile and phone up
ana_08.content: The biggest year-over-year shift is in how complaints get filed, not what they say. ONLINE share dropped 15 percentage points between 2023 and 2024 (68.8% → 53.5%), while MOBILE rose 8 pp (22.6% → 30.5%) and PHONE rose 7 pp (8.6% → 15.9%). In absolute terms ONLINE complaints actually fell by 69,000 even though the dataset grew overall, while MOBILE added 75,000 and PHONE more than doubled (59K → 120K). The mobile app and the dialled-in voice call are both gaining at the website's expense — a non-obvious result given the widespread story that 311 is going more digital.

data_table.description: Channel counts by year

ana_09.label: Borough share — Manhattan tops raw count, but the Bronx is loudest per capita
ana_09.content: By raw complaint volume the boroughs are close: Manhattan 26.9% (387,561), Brooklyn 26.2% (377,416), Bronx 24.7% (354,909), Queens 20.0% (287,977), Staten Island 2.2% (31,157). Per 1,000 residents the order flips dramatically: the Bronx files 241 complaints per 1,000 residents over two years, Manhattan 229, Brooklyn 138, Queens 120, and Staten Island only 63 — Staten Islanders complain less than one-quarter as much per person as Bronx residents. That ordering matches the recent TimeOut finding that the Bronx was the loudest borough by per-capita complaint rate in 2025.

ana_11.label: Top ZIPs per capita — 10466 logs more than one complaint per resident
ana_11.content: Scaling for population makes the 10466 outlier nearly unbelievable: 1,231 complaints per 1,000 residents over two years — more than one per person. Eleven of the next fourteen are split between Manhattan (six) and Brooklyn (four), with Queens contributing two and the Bronx three. The cluster in the 460s–680s per 1k (11414 Queens, 10023 Manhattan UWS, 10030/10031/10026/10034/10040 Harlem-Washington-Heights) is the more 'normal' per-capita ceiling — already ten times Staten Island's borough rate.

ana_12.label: Monthly seasonality — quiet in February, peak in spring 2023 and fall 2024
ana_12.content: Complaints follow the temperature: February is the quiet trough in both years (40K and 40K), May 2023 was the year's busiest month (75K), but in 2024 the pattern shifts — June was the May-equivalent peak (75K) and September was the absolute year-high (88K), almost double February's volume. The 2024 fall reload is almost entirely driven by ZIP 10466 (see ana_24/25): without that one ZIP, October–December 2024 looks like a normal year.

data_table.description: Monthly complaint counts, 2023 vs 2024

ana_13.label: Day of the week — Sunday is the loudest day of the week
ana_13.content: Sunday and Saturday between them carry 40.75% of every complaint — Sunday alone is 21.13% (304,195), Saturday 19.62% (282,440), Friday a clear third at 13.58%. The four weekdays Mon–Thu each sit between 10.7% and 12.6%, just below the 14.3% an even split would predict. The weekend wave starts Friday evening and crests on Sunday, when many of the previous night's parties get reported the next morning along with that day's brunch noise.

ana_14.label: Hour of day — 10 PM and 11 PM are the city's loudest hours; weekends extend the spike
ana_14.content: Across both years, 10 PM is the loudest hour (154,924 complaints), narrowly ahead of 11 PM (149,816). ana_15.label: The July 4 fireworks pulse — visible in 2023, much flatter in 2024
ana_15.content: In 2023 the late-June / early-July fireworks wave is clearly visible: June 24–25 produced 3,550 then 4,150 complaints (vs the dataset median of 1,684), and July 4 itself hit 3,607. In 2024 the spike spread out and softened — June 22–23 reached 2,974 then 3,359, and July 4 was 3,252 — slightly above an average day rather than the dramatic stand-out it was in 2023. The dataset contains no descriptor literally tagged 'firework' in 2023–2024 (fireworks roll into Banging/Pounding and other descriptors), so this pulse has to be read off the daily counts and the calendar rather than off a category.

data_table.description: Daily complaints, late-June to July 8, 2023 vs 2024

ana_16.label: Response time — NYPD closes in 41 minutes, DEP in 3 days, EDC takes 35 days
ana_16.content: Median time from created_date to closed_date varies by three orders of magnitude depending on the agency. NYPD closes the median noise complaint in 0.68 hours (41 minutes), and 90% of NYPD cases close within 3.91 hours. DEP, which handles construction and ice cream truck calls, takes a median 68.3 hours (2.85 days) with a p90 of 251.78 hours (10.5 days). EDC, which owns every helicopter complaint, takes a median 843.23 hours — over 35 days — to close a request, with a p90 of 2,746 hours (114 days). Across complaint types within each agency the response time is essentially flat, because what determines speed is who answers, not what the problem is.

ana_17.label: Resolution mix — 'no evidence of violation' closes one in three complaints

Another 4.11% (59,142) close as 'no one was at the location / unable to gain entry'. ana_19.label: Helicopter complaints fell 51% from 2023 to 2024 — opposite of the prior trend
ana_19.content: Despite the City Council's own data team reporting 59,127 helicopter-noise complaints for 2023, the 2024 number is just 28,686 — a 51.5% drop, the largest year-over-year decline of any complaint_type. Every single month except September is down year-over-year, often by half or more (May fell from 7,461 to 2,833; December fell from 8,724 to 2,843). This contradicts the prior 2020 → 2023 explosion documented by Stop the Chop and the Council, and is the strongest argument in the dataset that something changed around early 2024 — either filings tactics, public attention, or weather/flight volume — well before the 2025 Helicopter Oversight Act passed.

data_table.description: Helicopter-noise complaints by month, 2023 vs 2024

ana_20.label: Helicopter hotspots — 58% Manhattan, ZIP 10023 alone is 31%
ana_20.content: Helicopter complaints are spatially concentrated in a way the other categories are not. Manhattan files 57.8% of every helicopter complaint (50,743 of 87,813), Queens 23.9%, Brooklyn 16.8%, and the Bronx and Staten Island under 1% combined. The single ZIP 10023 — Upper West Side / Lincoln Center / Riverside Park — accounts for 27,539 complaints, 31% of all helicopter complaints citywide. The next biggest, 11414 in Howard Beach Queens (close to the JFK approach), files 16,646. This concentration aligns with the Council data team's hotspot list of Upper West Side, Murray Hill–Kips Bay, and the Carroll Gardens / Park Slope strip along the Hudson and East Rivers.

ana_21.label: Ice cream truck enforcement — 2,805 complaints, 15 actual violations issued
ana_21.content: The dataset has 2,805 complaints with the descriptor 'Noise, Ice Cream Truck (NR4),' all routed to DEP. Of those, 2,132 (76%) close with 'DEP didn't observe a violation of the NYC Air or Noise Code,' 554 (20%) are flagged as duplicates of earlier complaints, and exactly 15 (0.53%) actually close with 'DEP observed a violation.' The 1970s deal — jingles legal while the truck is moving, illegal while parked, fines $350–$3,000 — is essentially unenforced in practice; the rate of complaint-to-citation is roughly 1 in 187.

ana_22.label: What grew vs what shrank — Residential +27%, Helicopter -52%
ana_22.content: The 9.8% citywide growth from 2023 to 2024 (ana_02) hides large opposite swings inside each category. Residential noise grew 27.1% year-over-year (+80,843 complaints), Street/Sidewalk grew 10.5% (+15,552), and Vehicle was nearly flat (-4.7%). Commercial was essentially unchanged. The big outlier is Helicopter at -51.5% (-30,441) — the only category that fell sharply. The other minor categories (Park, House of Worship) barely moved. The story of the year-over-year change is: more residential noise reporting, less helicopter reporting.

ana_25.label: ZIP 10466 — one complaint every 17 seconds on its worst day, 99% via mobile app
ana_25.content: The 10466 anomaly isn't a slow drip — it's a series of huge bursts almost entirely funneled through the NYC311 mobile app. On Sunday 2024-09-15, the ZIP filed 4,952 complaints in 24 hours — one every 17.4 seconds, all day, every hour. 4,933 of those (99.6%) came through MOBILE; only 13 through the website and 6 by phone. Eight separate days in 2024 saw 3,000+ complaints from this single ZIP, all with the same channel distribution. The median day in 10466 is 12 complaints; on its top day it is 412× that. Across the eighteen days with 1,000+ complaints, the pattern is identical: an avalanche of mobile-app filings flagged 'Loud Music/Party,' suggesting an organized mass-filing or a very small group of repeat reporters rather than a real noise spike.

caveats.content: 311 measures who *reports* noise, not where noise actually is. A higher per-capita complaint rate in a ZIP code can reflect either more noise, more sensitivity, better internet/app access, or — as ZIP 10466's pattern suggests — a small number of high-volume repeat reporters. The dataset does not include any information about the person who filed the complaint.

Per-capita scaling uses 2020 ACS 5-year ZCTA population estimates, which approximate but do not exactly match the ZIP code boundaries the city's geocoder assigns to each complaint. The per-capita rankings are therefore approximate.

The dataset does not contain a complaint_type or descriptor literally tagged 'firework' for the 2023–2024 period — fireworks-related complaints get folded into 'Banging/Pounding' and other generic descriptors. The July-4 pulse (ana_15) is read from the daily count and the calendar, not from a category.

The 'NYPD: responded — took action / not necessary' bucket merges several similar resolution-description strings; the underlying texts vary. Treat the broad buckets as approximate aggregations rather than exact tallies of a single phrase.

Press reports of '610,000' or '738,000' noise complaints in 2024 use slightly different filters from this dataset (which counts every complaint_type containing 'Noise' as filtered server-side by SODA). Our 2024 total of 753,275 is the canonical count for the filter described in the manifest.
